One real project week (tlvphoto, 2026-07) shipped five bug classes past green suites. Each landed
as a standing rule; the review that folded them is recorded in
`docs/prover/2026-07-09-rows182-186.md`.

=== docs/worker-liveness.md:36 ===

Life on any one check means reconnect and treat the worker's files as claimed. A dead verdict requires all three quiet together — a still write-set, a stale heartbeat, and an unanswered probe — declared in one written line, then proceed. Until that verdict the worker's output is never framed as finished. A worker from a prior context counts as a foreign writer until verified; the same-session courtesy of the concurrent-edit fence ends at the wipe. No second worker goes onto a shared tree until the first has confirmed halted by its own reply or has been declared dead by all three checks (INV-11, INV-76).

Before a wipe, prefer halting the workers or letting them finish, so the next session starts single-writer. A handoff also says plainly when a worker dies with a closed window or a sleeping machine, so nobody is told the worker will simply be recognized. A worker puts a file back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any tree: `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and `git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. Such a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage lands on files the worker never wrote and its brief never named. This rule binds a worker in every tree, including its own isolated worktree, since a worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a worker cannot read off its brief what else that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes for a file it mutated, or that believes a file needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file and the mutation it made, and it writes no further file and runs no further command. The orchestrator owns recovery: it restores the named file from the last committed stage, hands the worker a fresh brief carrying that file's current bytes, and records the halt in the row's delivery report, and the halted work resumes under that new brief. ## 1. Restore-command implementation proposal (dry-run first)

### 1(a) — the canonical command, evaluated against the walk's own text

The walk is not a simple "no changes yet" precondition. By the time a restore would ever be invoked, Phase 3 has run: `MIGRATION.md:35` opens Phase 3 with "a clean-tree baseline commit," then step 4 (`MIGRATION.md:38`) applies steps that move, merge, and retire files, each producing further commits or working-tree changes under checkpoint discipline (`MIGRATION.md:37`). So "the pre-walk state" is a real prior commit, not just "uncommitted diffs to discard," and the candidates split on what they do to *history* versus *tree* versus *untracked files*:

| Command | What it does to the walk's commits | What it does to untracked files | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git reset --hard <baseline>` | Moves the branch pointer back, **discarding** every commit the walk made | Left alone — a new file the walk created (e.g. a plan doc under `.live-spec/adopt/` before it was committed, or an attic file written but not yet added) survives on disk | Returns tracked content to pre-walk bytes but can leave stray untracked debris; also the exact command family INV-298/299 (`PRODUCT_SPEC.md:7364`) forbids by name for a *worker* |
| `git checkout <baseline> -- .` | Leaves history alone, overwrites the working tree from the baseline's tree | Leaves untracked files alone (checkout only touches paths present in the source tree) | Wrong shape: it does not remove the walk's own commits from the branch, so "the host" still records a walk that ostensibly never happened on disk yet the commit graph disagrees — violates "returns the host to the pre-sequence state" for a host that would then `git log` its own supposedly-undone walk |
| `git revert <range>` | Adds new commits that undo each walk commit, keeping full history | Does nothing to untracked files; also does nothing for merges/renames the walk did with `git mv` semantics unless every step is cleanly revertible | Forward-only, so it does not "return" the tree in one command unless the range is a single squashed commit; also fragile against conflicting reverts if Phase 3 did file-content merges (`MIGRATION.md:65-69`, the preserve-and-re-home law) |
| `git restore --source=<baseline> --worktree --staged -- .` | No history change | Same gap as `checkout <baseline> -- .`: does not delete files new since baseline | Same shape problem as checkout; also does not exist as a bare one-liner that also cleans — needs a second command |

**Recommendation:** `git reset --hard <baseline>` **followed by** `git clean -fd -- .` is the only pairing that satisfies "the one command" in spirit while actually returning the host to the pre-sequence state on disk: `reset --hard` undoes the commits and tracked-file changes, `clean -fd` removes anything the walk created that never got committed (a half-written plan doc, a written-but-unadded attic file). Framed as one shell invocation it is one command line: `git reset --hard <baseline> && git clean -fd`. This is the literal command the walk's own prose gestures at but never writes down.

**The attic gap (PRODUCT_SPEC.md:4250):** "The attic *shall* keep every superseded file readable without any restore." This promise is orthogonal to, not a substitute for, the restore command: the attic guarantees a *retired* file stays readable in its new home after the walk lands (so a person doesn't need git archaeology to read something the walk moved). It says nothing about undoing the walk itself. `git reset --hard` would also roll back the attic commits, so a restored host loses the attic entries the walk wrote — which is correct (restore means the walk never happened) but worth stating explicitly in the plan-document sentence, since a reader could otherwise think the attic promise is itself the restore mechanism.

**The worked example that makes the untracked-file gap concrete:** if Phase 3 step 2 writes the pre-walk inventory (`MIGRATION.md:36`) into `.live-spec/adopt/` before the baseline commit's descendants ever `git add` it, and the walk is interrupted before that inventory file is committed, `git reset --hard <baseline>` alone leaves that inventory file sitting on disk, untracked — exactly the kind of "difference outside the plan" the before-and-after self-test (`MIGRATION.md:57`) is built to catch, except here it's the restore path leaving the mess, not the walk.

## 1. Restore-command implementation proposal (dry-run first)

### 1(a) — the canonical command, evaluated against the walk's own text

The walk is not a simple "no changes yet" precondition. By the time a restore would ever be invoked, Phase 3 has run: `MIGRATION.md:35` opens Phase 3 with "a clean-tree baseline commit," then step 4 (`MIGRATION.md:38`) applies steps that move, merge, and retire files, each producing further commits or working-tree changes under checkpoint discipline (`MIGRATION.md:37`). So "the pre-walk state" is a real prior commit, not just "uncommitted diffs to discard," and the candidates split on what they do to *history* versus *tree* versus *untracked files*:

| Command | What it does to the walk's commits | What it does to untracked files | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git reset --hard <baseline>` | Moves the branch pointer back, **discarding** every commit the walk made | Left alone — a new file the walk created (e.g. a plan doc under `.live-spec/adopt/` before it was committed, or an attic file written but not yet added) survives on disk | Returns tracked content to pre-walk bytes but can leave stray untracked debris; also the exact command family INV-298/299 (`PRODUCT_SPEC.md:7364`) forbids by name for a *worker* |
| `git checkout <baseline> -- .` | Leaves history alone, overwrites the working tree from the baseline's tree | Leaves untracked files alone (checkout only touches paths present in the source tree) | Wrong shape: it does not remove the walk's own commits from the branch, so "the host" still records a walk that ostensibly never happened on disk yet the commit graph disagrees — violates "returns the host to the pre-sequence state" for a host that would then `git log` its own supposedly-undone walk |
| `git revert <range>` | Adds new commits that undo each walk commit, keeping full history | Does nothing to untracked files; also does nothing for merges/renames the walk did with `git mv` semantics unless every step is cleanly revertible | Forward-only, so it does not "return" the tree in one command unless the range is a single squashed commit; also fragile against conflicting reverts if Phase 3 did file-content merges (`MIGRATION.md:65-69`, the preserve-and-re-home law) |
| `git restore --source=<baseline> --worktree --staged -- .` | No history change | Same gap as `checkout <baseline> -- .`: does not delete files new since baseline | Same shape problem as checkout; also does not exist as a bare one-liner that also cleans — needs a second command |

**Recommendation:** `git reset --hard <baseline>` **followed by** `git clean -fd -- .` is the only pairing that satisfies "the one command" in spirit while actually returning the host to the pre-sequence state on disk: `reset --hard` undoes the commits and tracked-file changes, `clean -fd` removes anything the walk created that never got committed (a half-written plan doc, a written-but-unadded attic file). Framed as one shell invocation it is one command line: `git reset --hard <baseline> && git clean -fd`. This is the literal command the walk's own prose gestures at but never writes down.

**The attic gap (PRODUCT_SPEC.md:4250):** "The attic *shall* keep every superseded file readable without any restore." This promise is orthogonal to, not a substitute for, the restore command: the attic guarantees a *retired* file stays readable in its new home after the walk lands (so a person doesn't need git archaeology to read something the walk moved). It says nothing about undoing the walk itself. `git reset --hard` would also roll back the attic commits, so a restored host loses the attic entries the walk wrote — which is correct (restore means the walk never happened) but worth stating explicitly in the plan-document sentence, since a reader could otherwise think the attic promise is itself the restore mechanism.

**The worked example that makes the untracked-file gap concrete:** if Phase 3 step 2 writes the pre-walk inventory (`MIGRATION.md:36`) into `.live-spec/adopt/` before the baseline commit's descendants ever `git add` it, and the walk is interrupted before that inventory file is committed, `git reset --hard <baseline>` alone leaves that inventory file sitting on disk, untracked — exactly the kind of "difference outside the plan" the before-and-after self-test (`MIGRATION.md:57`) is built to catch, except here it's the restore path leaving the mess, not the walk.
